passages.t: Passover: the night Israel was brought out
passages.happening:
Moses sets out the three great feasts of the year. The first is Passover. “Observe the month of Abib and celebrate the Passover to the LORD your God, because in the month of Abib the LORD your God brought you out of Egypt by night” (verse 1).

The Passover sacrifice is to be offered ‘in the place the LORD will choose as a dwelling for His Name’ (verse 2), and not in the towns (verse 5). It is offered in the evening, ‘as the sun sets, at the same time you departed from Egypt’ (verse 6).

For seven days the people eat bread made without leaven, which Moses calls ‘the bread of affliction, because you left the land of Egypt in haste’ (verse 3). The purpose is stated: ‘so that you may remember for the rest of your life the day you left the land of Egypt’. On the seventh day there is a solemn gathering, and no work is done (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Abib falls in March or April. The name comes from the fresh ears of barley that ripen then. After the exile Jews used the Babylonian name for the month, Nisan.

Passover goes back to the last night in Egypt, told in Exodus 12. Each family killed a lamb and marked its doorposts with the blood, and God passed over those houses. Israel left before morning.

Leaven is a piece of old fermented dough kept back to make the next batch rise. On the night of the exodus there was no time to wait for bread to rise. So the bread of the feast is flat, and Moses names it the bread of affliction. Every year the taste of it put Israel back in the hour of its escape.

The feast is about memory. The word ‘remember’ is the reason given in verse 3, and the timing in verse 6 is chosen to match the very hour. Israel did not only tell the story. It ate it.

Other peoples of the ancient world held feasts at the same seasons, tied to the gods they thanked for crops and herds. Israel's feasts took the same seasons and told a different story. They remembered a rescue.

After the temple was destroyed in AD 70, the Jewish Passover returned to the home, in the form of the Seder meal, without the sacrifice. It is kept to this day.
passages.later:
Exodus tells how the first Passover was eaten: “You are to eat in haste; it is the LORD’s Passover” (Exodus 12:11).

Jesus' family kept this law: “Every year His parents went to Jerusalem for the Feast of the Passover” (Luke 2:41). And on the night before he died Jesus said to his disciples, “I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering” (Luke 22:15).

Paul writes to the church, “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The New Testament draws that line. The feast itself remains at the heart of Jewish worship.
passages.hard:
In Exodus the Passover is a meal in each home. Here it must be offered at the one sanctuary. Why the difference?

In Exodus 12 the first Passover was kept in family houses in Egypt, with blood on each doorpost. This chapter forbids the sacrifice in the towns and requires it at the place God chooses.

Many scholars read this as a deliberate change that goes with the gathering of worship in one place. They connect it with the reform of King Josiah, of whose Passover it is said, “No such Passover had been observed from the days of the judges” (2 Kings 23:22).

Those who hold that the law comes from Moses generally read Exodus as describing the first Passover, which could happen only once, and Deuteronomy as giving directions for keeping it afterward, once Israel had a sanctuary in the land. They note that Numbers 9 already describes a Passover kept by the whole camp in the wilderness. Some add that the meal could still be eaten by families, while the sacrifice belonged at the sanctuary.

These notes take no side. In the time of Jesus both things were done. The lambs were killed at the temple in Jerusalem and eaten by families and groups in houses across the city.
passages.asks: Israel kept its rescue alive by acting it out every year, down to the taste of the bread. Ask what you do, regularly and with your body, to remember what God has done for you. And ask whether your faith has any fixed days in it, or only moods.

passages.t: Weeks and Tabernacles: joy for the whole household
passages.happening:
The second feast comes seven weeks after the first cutting of grain (verse 9). “And you shall celebrate the Feast of Weeks to the LORD your God with a freewill offering that you give in proportion to how the LORD your God has blessed you” (verse 10).

Everyone is to rejoice before God: sons and daughters, male and female servants, the Levite, ‘as well as the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widows among you’ (verse 11). “Remember that you were slaves in Egypt” (verse 12).

The third feast is the Feast of Tabernacles, seven days after the threshing floor and the winepress have been emptied (verse 13). The same list of people is to rejoice (verse 14). God will bless their harvest and their work, ‘so that your joy will be complete’ (verse 15).

Moses sums up. Three times a year the men are to appear before God at the place he chooses. “No one should appear before the LORD empty-handed” (verse 16). Each brings a gift ‘as he is able’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The three feasts follow the farming year. Passover came with the barley in spring. The Feast of Weeks came seven weeks later, at the end of the wheat harvest. The Feast of Tabernacles came in autumn, when the grapes and olives were in. A short Hebrew inscription called the Gezer Calendar, usually dated to the tenth century BC, lists the months by their farm work in a similar order.

In Greek the Feast of Weeks is called Pentecost.

‘Tabernacles’ are booths, small shelters of branches. The feast is named for the shelters Israel lived in during the wilderness years. Observant Jews still build booths for the festival today.

Two things stand out in these verses.

The first is that joy is commanded. Three times the chapter says ‘rejoice’. Worship in Deuteronomy is glad. A farmer brings in his crop, takes his household to God's house, and celebrates there.

The second is the guest list. Joy is not kept for those who own land. The servants are named. The Levite, who has no fields, is named. So are the foreigner, the orphan and the widow. These are the people who have no harvest of their own, and the law seats them at the feast. A family that celebrated alone had not kept it.

The reason is in verse 12. Israel had been slaves. People who remember having nothing know why the table has to be wide.

The gift is measured by what a person has received: ‘in proportion’, and ‘as he is able’. No fixed sum is named. The poor farmer and the rich one both come with something, and neither is shamed.
passages.later:
Leviticus explains the booths: ‘so that your descendants may know that I made the Israelites dwell in booths when I brought them out of the land of Egypt’ (Leviticus 23:43).

It was at the Feast of Weeks that the Holy Spirit was given to the first Christians: “When the day of Pentecost came, they were all together in one place” (Acts 2:1).

And at the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus stood in the temple and called out, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink” (John 7:37).
passages.asks: The law names the people who must be at the feast, and they are the ones with least. Ask who is at your table when you celebrate, and who never is. And ask whether gladness has a place in your worship, or whether you have come to think that seriousness and joy cannot go together.

passages.happening:
Moses turns from feasts to courts. “You are to appoint judges and officials for your tribes in every town that the LORD your God is giving you. They are to judge the people with righteous judgment” (verse 18).

Three things are forbidden. “Do not deny justice or show partiality. Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise and twists the words of the righteous” (verse 19).

Then the charge: “Pursue justice, and justice alone, so that you may live, and you may possess the land that the LORD your God is giving you” (verse 20).

Two short commands about worship follow. No wooden Asherah pole may be set up beside God's altar, and no sacred pillar, ‘which the LORD your God hates’ (verses 21-22).
passages.hearers:
Here a new part of the laws begins. Chapters 16 to 18 deal with those who hold authority in Israel: judges, kings, priests and prophets. Each is placed under God's law.

Justice is to be local. There are to be judges ‘in every town’. In an ancient village the town gate was the public square. The elders sat there to hear cases and settle quarrels. A poor person did not have to travel to find a court.

A judge who took bribes was a constant problem in the ancient world. Verse 19 says what a bribe does. It blinds. A wise man who takes one can no longer see the case in front of him. And it twists what honest people say.

In verse 20 the Hebrew says the word for justice twice: justice, justice you shall pursue. Doubling a word is a Hebrew way of adding weight. The verb is strong too. Justice is not something Israel may wait for. It is to be chased.

Israel's life in the land is tied to it: ‘so that you may live’. A people that lets its courts be bought will not last.

Verses 21 and 22 seem to change the subject. They do not. The Asherah pole and the standing stone were the furniture of Canaanite shrines. To set one beside the LORD's altar would be to blend his worship with theirs. In this book right worship and right judgment go together. A people that is careless about who God is will become careless about what is fair.
passages.later:
The law had said the same at Sinai: “Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds those who see and twists the words of the righteous” (Exodus 23:8).

The prophets found the courts of their day doing what this law forbids. Amos said, “You oppress the righteous by taking bribes; you deprive the poor of justice in the gate” (Amos 5:12). Micah said of Jerusalem, “Her leaders judge for a bribe, her priests teach for a price” (Micah 3:11).

Amos also gave the command of verse 20 its best-known form: “But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (Amos 5:24).
passages.asks: A bribe need not be money. Ask what can blind you when you have to judge between people: friendship, fear of someone powerful, or what you stand to gain. And ask whether you only approve of justice or go after it. The verse says to pursue.
